annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygon features represent individual housing-block/property objects of housing association ownership; not a full tessellation or reporting-unit layer. Numeric fields are attributes, while the mapped thing is the object itself.
Point layer of archaeological find locations/objects at specific addresses; the mapped feature is each archaeological site/object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual archaeological find locations/objects at specific places; the map is an object-based point layer, not measurements or events.
Polygon features mark selected archaeological sites/locations with addresses and site details; they are discrete mapped objects, not a full tessellation or area-wide patch layer.
Polygon areas mark where barbecue is allowed or forbidden, i.e. selected policy/restriction zones rather than a full tessellation or the park objects themselves.

Polygon areas for protected conservation/conservation-status zones; they are selected bounded areas where heritage protection applies, not a full tessellation or reporting units. PatchDS fits the preservation-area/affected-zone meaning.
Point geometry with year-stamped records of wild bee inventories/observations at locations; the decisive rule is EventDS for things that happened or were observed over time, not AmountDS.
Point locations with the main mapped phenomenon being the numeric count of bee colonies/hives per location (amount check), not the sites as objects.
Polygons form a zone-based map of diffuse soil quality; the layer describes applicable quality zones rather than discrete objects, so this is a tessellation with PatchDS.
Point geometry with 70k tree locations; each point is a distinct real-world object (a tree), not a measurement or event. Numeric fields are attributes, so ObjectDS.
Point geometries represent individual trees; the layer is about identifiable tree objects with species and planting attributes, not measurements or events.
Point geometry with 70k tree locations; the mapped thing is individual trees, so ObjectDS rather than AmountDS or ExistenceDS.
Point features represent individual trees as identifiable real-world objects; attributes like species, owner, and planting year are descriptive, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point features marking distinct compost initiatives at addresses/locations; the mapped thing is each initiative/object, not an event or measurement.
Polygons form a near-complete set of named areas for camera/overlast zones, so geometry is a tessellation and the main phenomenon is an area where the condition applies, which fits PatchDS.
Point features represent individual trees (mapped objects), with attributes like species, measures, and planning status; this is a point object layer, not a measurement/event/amount layer.
Point geometries mark individual sensor/camera installations; the mapped thing is the object itself, not a measurement or event.

The layer maps selected cultural-historical exploration areas and protected area boundaries, not a full tessellation. The polygons are bounded zones where heritage values/policies apply, so PatchDS fits better than ObjectDS or CoverageDS.
Point features represent mapped knotweed sightings/occurrences, a distinct real-world object (plant occurrence) rather than measurements, events, or a network.

Point features represent ecopassage/knelpunt locations and their planned or realized mitigation status; the layer is about ecological barriers and solutions at locations, so PointDS with EventDS for occurrences/planned realization.

Polygon regions are selected potential wind-energy areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon/applicability zones; numeric MW/GWh are attributes, not the main mapped phenomenon.

Point geometry with each feature representing a voting location/stemlocatie object; numeric vote fields are attributes, not the main phenomenon. This is an object layer for polling sites, not a point-measurement or amount layer.
Point geometry; each point marks a reported oak processionary caterpillar nest/location, so the mapped thing is a discrete object, not a measurement or event.

Polygon areas marked by pedicab permission/ban rules, so this is a selected restriction/policy area layer. The polygons do not form a full tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion; the decisive entity rule is PatchDS for applicability/restriction zones.
Point features marking pedicab and carriage stand locations; the mapped thing is the standplace itself, so ObjectDS.
Point features represent BAG addresses/objects with non-residential function classifications; this is a point-based object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

The polygons are block-street area units forming a near-complete tessellation, and the layer is a full-area categorical function mix classification (Wonen/Voorzieningen/Werken), so CoverageDS fits better than object or patch.
Neighborhood polygons form an administrative/reporting-unit partition of Amsterdam, so this is a vector tessellation and the entity is LatticeDS (wijken/buurten/stadsdelen as reporting units).

The layer maps Amsterdam neighborhoods/districts/areas as administrative reporting units, which forms a near-complete area partition, so the geometry is VectorTessellation and the entity is LatticeDS.
Neighborhood polygons form a reporting-unit tessellation (buurten/wijken/stadsdelen) used for geographic aggregation, so Geometry is VectorTessellation and Entity is LatticeDS.
Neighborhoods/buurten are reporting/statistical units that partition the city area, so the layer is a vector tessellation with lattice entities.
City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition the city; polygons form a tessellation, and the decisive rule is reporting-unit keywords -> LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative/reporting units that partition the city area, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is LatticeDS.
Administrative area layer of buurten/wijken/stadsdelen/gebieden forming a near-complete partition, so it is a tessellation of reporting units (LatticeDS).

Region polygons represent Amsterdam administrative/statistical areas (buurten, wijken, gebieden, stadsdelen) that partition the city; reporting-unit rule gives LatticeDS, and the polygon layer is a tessellation.

The layer is a set of Amsterdam practice/area units named like buurten, wijken, gebieden, and stadsdelen, which are reporting/administrative units forming a partition; numeric area is just an attribute.
Administrative/reporting area layer (buurten, wijken, gebieden, stadsdelen) forming a near-complete partition; classify as tessellation and reporting-unit lattice.

Polygon regions are selected noise-contour areas, not a tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS because the layer maps areas where noise levels apply (contours / affected zones), with dB values as attributes rather than the main entity.
Polygon isoline bands of noise levels (55-60 dB, 60-65 dB, etc.); this is a contour/value-class layer rather than objects or a tessellation.
Polygon noise contour bands are shown as interval/value classes (50–55, 55–60, etc.), so this is a contour layer; the polygons are not a full tessellation.
Polygon contour bands for noise levels (50–55 dB, 55–60 dB, etc.); this is a contour/isoline-style value class map, not a tessellation or object layer.
Point layer of polling locations/stembureaus; each point is a distinct voting location, and the numeric fields are election results attributes rather than the main phenomenon.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct green roof project/place at an address; the decisive rule is ObjectDS for identifiable real-world objects, not amount or patch.
Land use 2017 is an area-wide thematic classification of polygons, so the geometry is a tessellation and the entity is CoverageDS rather than object or patch.
Point geometries represent individual historical buildings/archeological sites, i.e. distinct mapped objects; the layer is object-focused rather than a measurement, event, or area classification.

Three standalone polygons are used as movable comparison shapes for Amsterdam boundaries, so this is not a tessellation. The mapped features are discrete bounded places/administrative objects (municipality, agglomeration, metro region), so ObjectDS fits best.
Polygon areas mark dog off-leash, ban, and restriction zones; they are selected applicability areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units. PatchDS is the decisive rule.

Polygon areas mark selected green-structure zones where policy and green functions apply, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon/policy areas; geometry is PlainVectorRegion because the polygons do not form a complete partition.
Point features represent individual elm trees (mapped objects), not measurements or events. The decisive rule is point objects, so Geometry=PointDS and Entity=ObjectDS.

Point features represent discrete student/youth housing projects and buildings, not measurements or events. Numeric woning counts are attributes of the housing objects, so the decisive rule is ObjectDS for identifiable facilities.
Point features represent individual bijzondere bomen (chestnut trees), so the decisive rule is points = PointDS and the mapped thing is a discrete real-world object = ObjectDS.
Point geometry with numeric climate/hydrology values sampled at locations; map is a measurement layer, so PointMeasuresDS.

Polygons represent flood-risk/overstroming zones from climate stress tests, not a full tessellation or discrete objects. The decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon areas, with PlainVectorRegion geometry because the areas do not form a complete partition.
Point features represent individual market locations (fixed places/facilities), not measurements or events; thus PointDS with ObjectDS.
Point geometry with named green monuments/bijzondere bomen; each point maps a distinct real-world object/place, not a measurement or network. Decision rule used: point objects -> ObjectDS.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct monumental tree object; numeric attributes are just properties, not the main mapped phenomenon.
Point features represent individual monuments/monument objects in Amsterdam; the layer is about identifiable monuments, not measurements or events.
Point locations mark current growth sites of protected/quay-wall plants; the layer is mainly about whether the species occurs at each location, with counts as secondary attributes.
Point layers of NO2 measurement locations; the main phenomenon is sampled air-quality concentration values at points, so PointDS and PointMeasuresDS apply.
Point locations are measurement sites for NO₂ concentrations; the layer is about sampled environmental measurements at points, not point objects.
Polygons mark the Oergeul as a bounded geological phenomenon/affected area, not a reporting unit or object; the map is about the extent of this area of concern (PatchDS).
Point layer of sonderingen/boreholes with sampled subsurface measurements; the main phenomenon is point-based measurement of a continuous geotechnical field, not objects or events.
Polygons represent named development neighbourhoods and stadsdelen, which are reporting/administrative units; this is a tessellation of area units, so VectorTessellation + LatticeDS.
Point features map distinct public toilet facilities and related amenities; this is an object layer, not measurements or events.
Polygon layer of 101 buurten/statistical areas; the decisive rule is reporting units, so entity is LatticeDS. The polygons also form a neighborhood tessellation across the city.

Polygon regions are selected areas for parking standards; the map describes area-specific rules applying to new construction, so this is a PatchDS. The polygons do not form a full-area tessellation, so Geometry is PlainVectorRegion.

Polygon layer of named parks/green spaces; not a reporting tessellation. The decisive rule is ObjectDS because the mapped features are identifiable parks and plantsoenen, with area as an attribute rather than the main phenomenon.
Polygon postcode4 areas are reporting units used to attach postcode attributes, and they are intended as a near-partition of the area, so this is VectorTessellation + LatticeDS.

Polygons are postcode-area units forming near-partitioned postcode4 regions, so VectorTessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units (postcode/buurt areas) -> LatticeDS, even though they are derived from address buffers.
Postcode6 polygon layer forms a near-complete tessellation of address-based postcode units; the decisive rule is reporting-unit / administrative-style areas, so LatticeDS.
LineString network of plus/main transport infrastructure; map describes prioritized road/transport networks, so NetworkDS is the decisive entity rule.

Polygon regions depict Amsterdam plus/hoofdnet pedestrian priority areas from a traffic-network policy layer; this is a selected applicability/priority zone, not a reporting unit or full tessellation. PatchDS fits the policy/affected area meaning.
Point geometry with named locations for cameras/sensors; the layer maps identifiable objects/places and privacy statements, not measurements or events.
Point geometry; each point is a concrete privacy-related site/camera/sensor or research location, so the feature is the mapped object rather than a measure or event.
Point locations mark specific cameras/sensors/privacy-scan sites; the layer is about identifiable objects/locations, not measurements or events.
Point geometries represent vote locations, and the main mapped phenomenon is numeric election results/circle sizes at those points, so PointDS + AmountDS.
Polygons are selected Rainproof problem/overlast areas from a 3Di model, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the decisive rule is PatchDS for bounded phenomenon areas.

Polygons are 67 hydro units that partition Amsterdam for Rainproof risk/overlast analysis, so the geometry is a tessellation; the mapped meaning is selected affected/attention zones from a 3Di model, which fits PatchDS rather than object or reporting-unit mapping.
Polygon layer of Amsterdam Rainproof bottleneck/overlast zones; the areas are selected phenomenon patches, not full coverage or reporting units, so VectorTessellation + PatchDS.

Polygons mark Rainproof problem/overlast areas from a 3Di simulation, so the mapped thing is a bounded phenomenon zone rather than a reporting unit or object; this fits PatchDS. The polygons do not form a full tessellation, so Geometry is PlainVectorRegion.
Point features mark identifiable religious buildings/locations with names and addresses, so this is PointDS with ObjectDS rather than amounts or events.
Line geometries map sidewalk segments, and the layer’s main phenomenon is sidewalk width/clearance as a numeric magnitude with obstacle-related values, so LineDS + AmountDS.

Line geometry with 1339 features; the layer maps the legal traffic-basis of 'snorfiets naar de rijbaan' as route/road segments where a restriction/applicability rule applies, so PatchDS fits better than ObjectDS or AmountDS.
Point features represent individual public sports facilities/playgrounds; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Point locations of city farming sites; each point represents a distinct real-world location/facility, so PointDS + ObjectDS.
Polygons are discrete named farming sites/parks with addresses and websites, so this is object mapping; they do not form a complete tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion.
Point features mark where initiatives/placements of the stadsloods occurred over time; the map is mainly about occurrences in years, so PointDS + EventDS.
Major streets are a connected street system, and all features are LineString geometries; decisive rule is NetworkDS for route/street infrastructure.
LineString transport layers for district heating/cooling networks; the decisive rule is connected infrastructure/route system, so Geometry is LineDS and Entity is NetworkDS.

Polygon buffers represent district heating/cooling network zones; metadata explicitly says transport lines were simplified and wijk lines buffered into polygons, so the mapped phenomenon is a network.
Polygon features represent named housing plan projects/areas with project names and max dwelling counts; this is a set of discrete planning objects, not a full tessellation or reporting-unit lattice.
Point features represent named local food initiatives/farms/shops at addresses; this is a point object layer, not measurements or events.
LineString features represent the tram/metro line network; metadata explicitly says it visualizes stations, stops, and lines, so the decisive rule is network infrastructure.
LineString features representing tram/metro routes and stops network; map description explicitly says it visualizes the network of stations, stops, and lines, so NetworkDS with LineDS geometry.
Point features represent tram stops and metro stations, but the layer’s main phenomenon is the tram/metro network of stops and lines, so NetworkDS wins over ObjectDS.
Point features represent tram stops/metro stations, but the layer’s main meaning is the transit network of stations, stops, and lines, so NetworkDS is the decisive entity.
Point features represent individual traffic-light-regulated intersections (distinct mapped objects), not measurements or events; point geometry with object meaning.
Line features are road links, and the mapped phenomenon is traffic intensity/prognosis on those links; numeric volumes are the main mapped values, so this is a line AmountDS layer.
Point features are stemlocaties (polling locations). The layer’s main message is vote counts/percentages per location, so the decisive rule is point AmountDS rather than object or event.
Point features represent individual trees (tree replacement layer); the decisive rule is object-by-point mapping, not amounts or events.
Point features represent distinct traffic information system objects (cameras, DRIP, signs, pollers) with standplaats and object IDs; this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point geometry with each feature representing a distinct traffic information system object/facility; metadata says the map shows nearly all such objects and clicking a point reveals object details.

Point features mark individual bird nesting locations/observations at addresses, so geometry is PointDS. The main phenomenon is mapped breeding bird residence sites as distinct locations, not a continuous measure or event, so ObjectDS.
Point geometry with 289 features, each point is a distinct bench in Vondelpark; metadata shows adoption status is an attribute, so the mapped thing is the object (bench), not an amount or event.
LineString features map street-segment walkability/sidewalk width conditions, not a route network; the layer is a bounded phenomenon area for pedestrian policy/conditions, so PatchDS fits best.
Point features map discrete wall art objects at specific building addresses; this is an inventory of identifiable cultural objects, not measurements or events.

Polygon regions encode Amsterdam welstand levels (policy/applicability zones) that partition the city area, so geometry is a tessellation and the entity is PatchDS because the mapped thing is the area where a welstand regime applies.

Polygons form a citywide classification of welstand/beauty policy areas with levels applying to areas, so this is a tessellated region layer and the entity is best treated as a patch/policy zone rather than individual objects.
Point locations mark WWII attack/incident occurrences with dates; this is an event layer on points rather than objects or measurements.

Polygons represent housing development projects, but the map’s main phenomenon is the numeric plan supply (Totaal and housing counts) and staged start years. This is a polygon amount layer rather than a tessellation or reporting-unit map.
Point layer of identifiable self-build plot projects/facilities; the mapped thing is each project/plot location, not a measurement or event.

Polygons are used as a citywide partition of building/dask areas by solar-panel opportunity categories, so geometry is a tessellation; the main phenomenon is a bounded applicability/constraint zone on heritage roofs, best treated as PatchDS rather than objects.
Point features represent detected solar-panel systems, and the layer’s main message is numeric magnitude (count of panels and estimated capacity in Wp), so PointDS with AmountDS.
Point geometry with named swimming locations and facilities; the mapped thing is the place/object itself, not a measurement or network.
